items.title: 2027 UTME: JAMB moves to shut down substandard CBT centres
items.description: By Joseph Erunke The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) has moved to tighten its grip on the conduct of the 2027 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME), warning that computer-based test (CBT) centres that fail to meet its prescribed standards will be denied accreditation. The Board said only centres with adequate facilities, reliable infrastructure and the operational capacity to guarantee a credible and hitch-free examination would be approved to host candidates in the 2027 exercise. JAMB Registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, gave the indication during a meeting with the leadership of the Chief External Examiners, where preparations and readiness for the accreditation exercise ahead of the 2027 UTME were reviewed. According to a post on the Board’s official X handle on Thursday, the meeting was part of efforts to strengthen examination administration and ensure strict compliance with established operational standards. The Board said the accreditation exercise would serve as a critical screening mechanism to prevent inadequately equipped centres from participating in the examination, thereby protecting candidates from avoidable disruptions and compromising examination conditions. Reiterating its position, JAMB declared that accreditation would not be automatic for CBT centres seeking to participate in the exercise. “Only centres that meet JAMB’s standards will be accredited to host the examination. For candidates, that means a fair and secure place to sit the UTME, wherever they write it,” the Board stated. The development signals JAMB’s determination to strengthen the credibility of the UTME by ensuring that candidates, irrespective of their examination locations, have access to a secure, reliable and conducive testing environment. The strict accreditation regime is also expected to address operational shortcomings that have historically threatened the smooth conduct of computer-based examinations, including inadequate facilities and poor technical readiness. With preparations for the 2027 UTME gathering momentum, the Board maintained that compliance with its accreditation requirements would remain non-negotiable for all CBT centres seeking approval to participate in the nationwide examination. items.title: Dette extérieure Sénégal : 45,399 milliards de dollars enregistrés en 2025
items.description: Au Sénégal, l’encours total de la dette extérieure a atteint 45,399 milliards de dollars en 2025, soit plus de 26 531 milliards de francs CFA. Ce qui représente une hausse de 10 % par rapport à 2024. C’est ce que révèle le Rapport sur la dette internationale 2026 du Groupe de la Banque mondiale rendu public le jeudi 5 novembre 2026. L’encours total de la dette extérieure du Sénégal est estimé à 45,399 milliards de dollars en 2025, soit plus de 26 531 milliards de francs CFA, soit une hausse de 10 % par rapport à 2024. Selon le Rapport sur la dette internationale 2026 du Groupe de la Banque mondiale publié le 5 novembre 2026, il a plus que quadruplé depuis 2015, où il s’établissait à 10 470 millions. L’analyse des tableaux de cette dette montre que la courbe progresse de façon quasi continue, avec un léger repli autour de 2023-2024 avant la reprise de 2025. Ainsi, concernant la structure par débiteur, le document souligne que la dette se répartit en trois grandes catégories. A lire aussi : Dette extérieure des pays en développement : un montant record de 9 400 milliards de dollars en 2025 Celle publique et garantie par l’État a atteint 29,589 milliards de dollars, environ 65 % du total. La dette privée non garantie est de 13,101 milliards, environ 29 % et celle à court terme est estimée à 2,709 milliards de dollars, soit 6 % du montant global. Il convient de noter que le poids de la dette privée non garantie est notable. Elle ne bénéficie pas de la garantie de l’État, mais pèse sur la position extérieure globale du pays. Il urge aussi de noter que, des données de la Banque mondiale, il ressort de la structure par type de créancier sur la dette publique et garantie trois catégories. Pour les créanciers multilatéraux, le montant est d’environ 13,287 milliards de dollars, soit 45 %. Concernant des créanciers privés et bilatéraux, le Sénégal leur doit respectivement 11,108 milliards de dollars et 5,193 milliards de dollars. Sur la liste des créanciers multilatéraux, la Banque mondiale à travers l’IDA est le premier créancier avec 5,186 milliards de dollars, suivie de la Banque africaine de développement (BAD) avec 2,135 milliards de dollars et d’autres institutions multilatérales qui cumulent 5,967 milliards de dollars de ces créances. Par rapport aux bilatéraux, le rapport indique que la Chine arrive en tête avec 2,086 milliards de dollars, devant la France à qui le Sénégal doit 1,611 milliard de dollars et les autres créanciers bilatéraux qui ont prêté 1,497 milliard à l’État sénégalais. Près de 38 % de la dette publique due à des créanciers privés Il urge aussi de noter, selon le document de la Banque mondiale, que près de 38 % de la dette publique est due à des créanciers privés (typiquement des détenteurs d’euro-obligations), ce qui expose le pays aux conditions des marchés financiers, généralement plus coûteuses que les financements concessionnels. Les graphiques montrent également que ces ratios ont augmenté sur la décennie, avec un pic marqué du service de la dette avant une forte décrue en 2025. Le niveau reste toutefois nettement supérieur à la fourchette interquartile qui se situe entre 25 et 75 % des pays déclarants, représentée par la bande grisée. Le Sénégal se situe donc parmi les pays les plus endettés de l’échantillon. Sur les conditions des nouveaux engagements en 2025, la Banque mondiale informe que pour les créanciers officiels, les nouveaux engagements ont en moyenne une maturité de 13 ans ; un différé d’amortissement de 4 ans et un taux d’intérêt de 3,0 %. Mariama DIEME

items.title: Aïssata Tall Sall : « Qu’on dissolve cette Assemblée et qu’on organise des élections législatives anticipées »
items.description: Aïssata Tall Sall préconise un retour aux urnes. La présidente du groupe parlementaire Takku-Wallu Sénégal appelle le chef de l’État à dissoudre l’Assemblée nationale et à convoquer des élections législatives anticipées. Selon elle, le peuple doit être appelé à arbitrer le différend entre l’Exécutif et le Législatif autour de l’adoption du budget 2027. La responsable politique justifie cette demande par ce qu’elle considère comme un blocage du débat démocratique au sein de l’Hémicycle. Elle dénonce notamment le refus, selon elle, de débattre du budget de la nation et l’utilisation du règlement intérieur pour limiter la parole de l’opposition. « Quand une institution refuse de débattre du budget de la nation, quand une majorité utilise le règlement intérieur non pour éclairer mais pour étouffer la parole, alors la seule issue démocratique, c’est le peuple », soutient-elle. Aïssata Tall Sall invite ainsi le président de la République à prendre ses responsabilités. « Qu’on dissolve cette Assemblée et qu’on organise des élections législatives anticipées », lance-t-elle, convaincue que les Sénégalais doivent « arbitrer eux-mêmes » la crise institutionnelle. « Un acte de salubrité démocratique » La présidente du groupe Takku-Wallu Sénégal présente cette dissolution comme une réponse démocratique à l’impasse actuelle, et non comme une manœuvre politicienne. « Nous ne craignons pas le verdict des urnes. C’est Pastef qui le craint, parce qu’il sait que son bilan budgétaire ne résistera pas à la campagne. Qu’ils assument leurs chiffres devant le peuple, s’ils en ont le courage », déclare-t-elle. Tout en rejetant l’idée de contribuer à un blocage des institutions, son groupe refuse également de soutenir la majorité parlementaire. Me Aïssata Tall Sall revendique ainsi une posture de « responsabilité républicaine » : contester la gestion du pouvoir sans, pour autant, prendre part à une paralysie du pays. Elle estime que le président de la République, élu avec 54 % des suffrages, doit prendre l’initiative de sortir de cette crise. « Si ce pays est bloqué, le premier qui aura violé son serment, ce ne sera pas nous », prévient-elle. C.G.D

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026-Futsal féminin : battu par l’Ukraine (7-2), le Sénégal éliminé dès les poules
items.description: Pour les Lioncelles, l'aventure olympique s'arrête net. Opposé à l'Ukraine pour son dernier match de groupe, à Iba-Mar-Diop, le Sénégal de Wolimata Seye s'est écroulé (7-2) ce 05 novembre 2026 alors qu'une victoire était indispensable pour viser les demi-finales . Après sa courte défaite face au Venezuela (0-1), l'équipe avait aligné Mariama et Marieme Niang d'entrée et dominait les premiers échanges. Mais sur une balle perdue par Mariama Faty, l'Ukraine a ouvert le score par Alina Hordiienko, contre le cours du jeu. Un but contre son camp de cette même Hordiienko a ramené le Sénégal à hauteur, sans que le Complexe IMD ne s'enflamme. La suite a été pénible. Oksana Chevchuk a repris l'avantage après une main ratée d'Awa Baldé, puis Marharyta Ruchka (15e) et Valeriia Yukhnovets (18e) ont fait le break. Hordiienko (24e) et Ruchka (25e) ont encore alourdi la note. Face à elles, la gardienne ukrainienne Kira Hulenko a tout repoussé : 25 arrêts, un record pour une gardienne depuis le début de ces JOJ. Bousso Diallo a bien réduit l'écart (38e), mais Ruchka a signé son triplé juste après (40e). Avec une victoire 8-1 contre les Fidji et deux revers, les Sénégalaises finissent troisièmes de leur poule avec 3 points. Le futsal féminin sénégalais, très récent, disputait seulement son deuxième tournoi international après la CAN 2025, où il n'avait pas dépassé les poules. Cette campagne reste une étape formatrice pour un groupe jeune, confronté à un niveau élevé. O.B.N

Speaking at the event at the Kempinski Hotel in Accra, she highlighted the importance of building human competence, particularly in critical thinking, communication, public speaking and relationship-building. “You have to build the competence before you transform,” she said. Ms Kwaku-Dosoo challenged participants to shift their focus from celebrating the achievements of others to developing themselves into people whose lives and work can inspire others. She said personal transformation required more than motivation, stressing that individuals must deliberately invest in the skills and abilities needed to achieve their goals. items.title: Gavin Newsom’s Big Move on the Death Penalty
items.description: Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced that he will commute the sentences of every prisoner on the state’s death row—548 people in all. With this action, Newsom could effect the largest-ever reduction of America’s death-row population, dropping the national total by about 27 percent. (California’s supreme court must approve some of the clemency requests.) California last executed a prisoner in 2006, and in 2019 Newsom instituted a moratorium against the death penalty via executive order. But in both 2012 and 2016, Californians narrowly voted against ballot measures that would have repealed the state’s death penalty, meaning many in the state would still prefer to see it in use. Newsom’s commutation order could foreclose that possibility in at least the near future. Newsom’s commutations underscore how polarized the country has become on the death penalty. Although several states have rejected capital punishment in recent years, a handful of red states are pushing back against that trend, taking ever more extreme measures to hand down death sentences and carry out executions. America’s death-penalty landscape is defined by dueling philosophies, which means that prisoners convicted of capital crimes face radically different outcomes depending on minor changes in geography: The fate of the same person committing the same murder on either side of the border between Texas, where executions are relatively common, and New Mexico, which does not permit capital punishment, would come down to only a few miles. The death penalty in America could grow ever more arbitrary and cruel before it dissolves altogether. [ From the July 2025 issue: Inside America’s death chambers ] State executives across the country have undertaken commutation actions similar to Newsom’s in recent years. When Colorado’s legislature abolished the state’s death penalty in 2020, Governor Jared Polis commuted all remaining death sentences; likewise, Governor Kate Brown commuted the death sentences of everyone on Oregon’s death row in 2022. In 2024, North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper issued 15 death-row commutations, reducing the state’s death-row population by roughly 10 percent. That same year, President Biden commuted the death sentences of 37 prisoners, leaving only three still facing death at the hands of the federal government. As of 2023, Governor Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions by issuing reprieves for every death warrant that comes across his desk. And earlier this year, Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a moderate Republican, granted his first death-row commutation and publicly urged his state’s legislature to abolish capital punishment altogether. Newsom’s intervention could give this trend considerable momentum. This pattern is in some respects unsurprising. The death penalty has been in a long-term decline for decades: Support for capital punishment for murder dropped from 80 percent during the 1990s to somewhere between 52 percent and 66 percent currently, depending on the phrasing of polling questions. ( Pew has detected a slight uptick in recent years.) In 1986, 325 new death sentences were handed down by juries across the country; in 2025, juries sentenced fewer than 30 prisoners to die, thanks in part to declining crime rates, criminal-justice reform efforts, and wide publicization of death-row exonerations. In recent years, several states have legislatively abolished the death penalty: New Hampshire in 2019, Colorado in 2020, Virginia in 2021, Washington in 2023, and Delaware in 2024, bringing the number of abolitionist states to 23. And the death penalty’s prospects going forward are dimming; younger generations are less likely to support it than their predecessors. America seems closer than ever to joining 74 percent of countries globally that have abandoned the death penalty—almost, but not quite. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Donald Trump dreams of more executions ] Use of the death penalty today is concentrated in a handful of traditionally red states, among them Texas, Florida, Oklahoma, Alabama, and Missouri, which together carried out roughly 68 percent of the country’s executions in 2025. Florida in particular has undergone a death-penalty renaissance in recent years, ratcheting up annual executions over the past two years, no longer requiring juries to hand down death sentences unanimously, and permitting the use of capital punishment to include non-homicide offenses such as the sexual assault of children. The Trump administration has also encouraged states to pursue the death penalty and has sought more federal death sentences following Biden’s mass commutations. This year, Tennessee severely botched the attempted executions of Tony Carruthers and Christa Pike . Roughly a week after Pike survived the gruesome efforts to kill her, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the Trump administration planned to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan , a prisoner on federal death row. More such horrors are still to come. But these incidents generated significant news coverage and, in Hasan’s case, mass public disapproval. Tennessee recently halted all executions, and the Trump administration backed away from livestreaming Hasan’s killing, though he will still be executed by firing squad. Reactionary efforts to shore up the death penalty might, in the end, help accelerate its decline.

items.title: I built a $70m business while battling depression – Nekeya Parks at TrueLife Experience
items.description: Mindset mentor Nekeya Parks has revealed that she built a $70 million business while battling depression, urging people to identify and pursue what she described as their God-given purpose. Speaking at the 2026 TrueLife Experience at the Kempinski Hotel in Accra, she challenged participants to reflect on the ambitions they had before societal expectations and personal fears influenced their choices. “When you think about the dream that you had when you were smaller, when you were younger, before the world got its hands on you, before all the reasons why it felt too big landed, what was your original dream?” she asked. Ms Parks said many people were raised to pursue conventional career paths such as engineering, medicine and law because they were considered secure and financially rewarding. However, she argued that these choices did not necessarily reflect an individual’s personal calling or purpose. “But that was not automatically the thing that God had placed within you. That’s the dream that I’m talking about, the thing that felt like it was what you needed to do, what you were put on this earth to do, and what God had called you to do,” she said. ‘My biggest audacity’ Ms Parks said her greatest act of courage was believing that she deserved a fulfilling and prosperous life despite the difficulties and experiences that shaped her upbringing. “My biggest audacity was believing that no matter what my people, my parents endured, no matter how unworthy I was taught that I was, I had audacity to believe that God wanted me to have a life that was healthy, rich, and that I loved,” she said. She disclosed that she built a business valued at $70 million while struggling with depression, highlighting the difference between financial success and personal fulfilment. “I built a $70 million business depressed. I had six and seven figures in a bank account, and I didn’t want to get out of bed most nights,” she said. ‘Hustle is not enough’ Ms Parks, whose mother is from Jamaica, said she grew up with an emphasis on hard work, financial success and security. She noted, however, that financial achievements alone might not bring fulfilment if individuals were not pursuing work aligned with their sense of purpose. “But if you are not doing that thing that God has placed within you, it is not going to lead to a feeling of bliss and happiness,” she said. The 2026 TrueLife Experience is a two-day gathering bringing together business executives, entrepreneurs, policymakers, professionals and emerging leaders to discuss courage, personal development and purposeful action. Other speakers at the event included business leader Sir Sam Jonah, Edward Effah, founder of Fidelity Group, and Dzigbordi Kwaku-Dosoo.

items.title: SEGMA : des recettes propres à 181,59 % des prévisions en 2025
items.description: Les Services de l’État gérés de manière autonome (SEGMA) ont dégagé, à fin 2025, un excédent de recettes d’environ 4 887,04 millions de dirhams (MDH), alors que leur nombre est revenu de 171 à 161 en 2026. Le rapport qui accompagne le projet de Loi de Finances n°60.26 pour 2027 dresse l’état des lieux de ces structures, dont la santé et l’enseignement constituent le cœur d’activité. Le rapport consacré aux SEGMA, joint au projet de Loi de Finances n°60.26 pour l’année budgétaire 2027, présente ces services comme un levier essentiel de la gestion budgétaire publique. Leur autonomie financière repose sur la mobilisation de recettes propres, issues des prestations rendues aux usagers. Elle leur donne, souligne le document, une plus grande réactivité et une gestion de proximité, en particulier dans les domaines de l’enseignement et de la santé. Le rapport, résumé par la Direction du Budget du ministère de l’Économie et des Finances, s’articule en trois volets : l’évolution du nombre de SEGMA en 2026, le bilan financier de 2025 comparé à celui de 2024, puis les réalisations physiques de 2025 et les plans d’action de 2026 et de 2027. Sur le plan des effectifs, les SEGMA s’établissent à 161 en 2026, contre 171 l’année précédente. Cette baisse découle de la suppression de onze services et de la création d’un seul, le « Service de la logistique et du matériel d’Errachidia », rattaché au ministère de l’Équipement et de l’Eau. Les suppressions touchent notamment le Centre national de transfusion sanguine et d’hématologie, le Centre régional de transfusion sanguine de Casablanca, la Direction du médicament et de la pharmacie et le Service de logistique et de matériel de Meknès. Elles concernent aussi plusieurs centres hospitaliers, régional à Tanger, provinciaux à Al Hoceima, Tétouan, Larache, Chefchaouen et Ouezzane, et préfectoral à M’diq-Fnideq. Trois autres SEGMA ont par ailleurs changé de dénomination. Le Centre de publication et de documentation judiciaire de la cour de cassation, relevant du ministère de la Justice, devient le « Centre de publication de l’information juridique ». Le Service de la formation continue du ministère de l’Équipement et de l’Eau se nomme désormais « Centre d’accueil et de conférences ». Le Centre de qualification professionnelle hôtelière et touristique de Touarga, à Rabat, devient l’« Institut spécialisé de technologie appliquée hôtelière et touristique de Touarga – Rabat », au sein du ministère du Tourisme, de l’Artisanat et de l’Économie solidaire. Les 161 SEGMA inscrits à la loi de finances 2026 se répartissent en huit domaines d’intervention, calqués sur les grandes fonctions de l’État. La santé en regroupe 81, devant l’enseignement, la formation professionnelle et la formation des cadres, qui en compte 45. Viennent ensuite l’équipement, le transport et les autres infrastructures économiques (16 services), les autorités publiques et services généraux (9), les activités récréatives (4), les autres activités sociales (3), l’agriculture et la pêche maritime (2) et les autres activités économiques (un seul service). Cette ventilation consacre la prédominance des SEGMA à caractère social, qui représentent 80,2 % du total, soit 129 services sur 161. Côté finances, le bilan de 2025 fait ressortir des recettes globales d’environ 7 769,28 MDH, pour des prévisions de 6 725,54 MDH, soit un taux de réalisation de 115,52 %. La performance la plus marquée concerne les recettes propres, qui ont atteint 3 025,31 MDH contre 1 665,99 MDH de prévisions actualisées, soit un taux de réalisation de 181,59 %. Le rapport relève aussi que les dotations d’équilibre versées par le budget général à certains SEGMA ont grimpé à 427,77 MDH en 2025, contre 356,46 MDH un an plus tôt, soit une hausse de l’ordre de 20 %. Le document précise que le montant global des recettes propres dépasse celui des dépenses totales. Le recours aux subventions s’explique, selon lui, par l’insuffisance des recettes propres de certains services pour couvrir l’intégralité de leurs dépenses. Quant aux excédents d’exploitation et d’investissement à fin 2024, reportés en complément des crédits de 2025, ils s’élèvent à 4 316,18 MDH, contre 3 857,41 MDH à fin 2023, soit une progression de 11,89 %. Du côté des dépenses, les émissions de 2025 se sont chiffrées à 2 882,22 MDH, pour des crédits ouverts de 6 468,86 MDH, soit un taux d’émission global de 44,56 %. Les dépenses d’exploitation émises atteignent 2 479,64 MDH, tandis que celles d’investissement s’établissent à environ 402,58 MDH. Le taux de couverture des dépenses par les recettes propres ressort ainsi à 104,96 % en 2025, contre 103,81 % en 2024, soit un gain de 1,15 point. Le rapport y voit la traduction d’une trajectoire vers une autonomie financière mieux maîtrisée. La troisième partie du rapport s’attache aux réalisations physiques, mesurées à partir d’indicateurs de production ou d’activité, afin d’apprécier la qualité des prestations offertes aux usagers. Dans la santé, les hôpitaux publics ont poursuivi les missions de supervision et de suivi des plans d’amélioration des établissements ayant fait l’objet d’inspections, lesquelles ont porté sur 50 établissements. Les efforts ont également visé les prestations de la médecine légale, la gestion des morgues, ainsi que le renforcement du système de réponse aux urgences pré-hospitalières et aux situations de catastrophe. En 2027, cette dynamique doit se poursuivre afin de rendre l’offre hospitalière accessible, disponible et globale, avec des soins sûrs et de qualité, et de remédier aux dysfonctionnements de l’hôpital public. Le rapport cite notamment l’évaluation de la performance des établissements et la communication des résultats aux directions régionales. Dans l’enseignement, la formation professionnelle et la formation des cadres, les réalisations ont porté sur la qualité de la formation dispensée aux étudiants. Elles ont notamment consisté à mettre en œuvre les feuilles de route de formation élaborées dans le cadre de la stratégie nationale de création d’emploi, à diversifier les filières en tenant compte de l’approche genre, et à améliorer les conditions d’accueil des élèves et des usagers par l’entretien et le nettoyage des locaux. Pour 2027, les actions prévues misent sur la diversification de l’offre de formation, l’élargissement des partenariats, de la coopération et de la recherche scientifique, ainsi que l’acquisition de matériel pédagogique destiné à cette recherche. Les SEGMA de l’équipement, du transport et des autres infrastructures économiques ont, sur 2025-2026, œuvré à la pérennité de la circulation sur le réseau routier. Ils ont notamment ausculté plus de 31 700 km de routes et développé le Système d’Information Routière (SIR) ainsi que le Système de Gestion du Relevé Visuel (SGRV). Ils ont aussi amélioré le contrôle des travaux routiers, aménagé des pistes rurales et entretenu les accotements. Pour 2027, les priorités annoncées sont la modernisation du système d’auscultation routière, le développement de la recherche technique et de l’innovation dans l’infrastructure routière, le renforcement du dispositif de suivi et de surveillance du trafic maritime et l’amélioration de la gouvernance du secteur de la météorologie. items.title: Delta Airlines : 1,1 million de passagers transportés entre Dakar et les États-Unis en 20 ans
items.description: Lancée en 2006, la liaison aérienne de Delta Airlines entre Dakar et les États-Unis célèbre cette année ses vingt ans d’existence. À cette occasion, la compagnie américaine a organisé, hier, une conférence de presse au King Fahd Palace, animée par son Directeur général à Dakar, Ryan Bowman. L’occasion a été saisie pour revenir sur le bilan de cette desserte et ses perspectives. Depuis son lancement, cette ligne a permis de transporter plus de 1,1 million de passagers. Elle accueille différentes catégories de voyageurs, notamment des membres de la diaspora, des hommes d’affaires, des diplomates, des étudiants et des touristes. Au-delà du transport aérien, cette desserte participe au renforcement des échanges entre le Sénégal et les États-Unis, tout en offrant des possibilités de correspondance vers d’autres destinations, a d’emblée souligné Ryan Bowman. Il a également mis en avant le rôle des partenariats noués sur le marché sénégalais dans le développement de cette liaison. La présence de Delta Airlines au Sénégal s’est également accompagnée d’initiatives en matière d’emploi et de formation. La compagnie indique « recruter du personnel local et proposer des stages rémunérés de douze mois à des étudiants de troisième cycle. En 2023, elle a notamment organisé, avec le Consortium Jeunesse Sénégal, un programme d’innovation ayant réuni 69 jeunes autour de thématiques liées à l’entrepreneuriat et au développement des compétences ». Abordant les contraintes du secteur aérien, le directeur général a évoqué notamment « la hausse des prix du pétrole, qui affecte l’ensemble des compagnies ». Selon lui, ces évolutions imposent une capacité d’anticipation et d’adaptation pour préserver la continuité des opérations. Après deux décennies de présence, la liaison Dakar–États-Unis constitue ainsi l’un des principaux axes de la desserte aérienne internationale du Sénégal. Mamadou Laye Dieye

items.title: Sir Sam Jonah shares life lessons on courage, humility and character at TrueLife Experience
items.description: Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has recounted how his upbringing in the mining town of Obuasi shaped his understanding of inequality, humility and respect for others. Speaking at the 2026 TrueLife Experience at the Kempinski Hotel in Accra on November 5, he reflected on the social and economic inequalities he observed growing up in the mining community. Held under the theme “The Audacity to Dare” , the two-day event brought together business executives, entrepreneurs, policymakers, professionals and emerging leaders to discuss personal development, leadership and purposeful action. Sir Sam Jonah said although wealth was being generated through gold mining in Obuasi, he observed that the people undertaking some of the hardest work did not necessarily have a corresponding say in how that wealth was managed. “I was born in Chile at the military camp. But Obuasi was the world in which I grew up. For those who don’t know Obuasi, it is a mining town, gold mining town,” he said. “Growing up, I could see that wealth was being produced around us. I could also see that the people doing some of the hardest work, they didn’t necessarily have the greatest say about it. I didn’t have the language to describe all the inequalities I was observing, but I could see them.” Lessons from his parents Sir Sam Jonah also credited his parents with instilling values that have guided his personal and professional life, particularly humility and respect for others. He said his mother taught him that personal achievements should never be used as an excuse for arrogance or disrespectful behaviour. “My mother had no patience for arrogance. You could achieve something impressive but that is not the right or permission to become unpleasant. It certainly did not excuse you from treating another person with respect,” he said. He also recalled his father’s advice that people do not choose the circumstances into which they are born, and that differences in opportunities should encourage understanding rather than a sense of superiority. “My father reminded me that the circumstances to which we were born are largely an accident. You didn’t select your parents. Our opportunities or advantages may make our journey easier,” he said. He added that this understanding should make people cautious about looking down on others who may not have enjoyed similar opportunities. Conduct reflects upbringing The business leader further emphasised the importance of character, saying a person’s behaviour reflects the values instilled in them. “There was a very powerful idea which was on our home. People ask about the home you come from. Your conduct says something about your upbringing,” he said. The 2026 TrueLife Experience featured other speakers, including mindset mentor Nekeya Parks and Edward Effah, founder of Fidelity Group.

items.title: Tamba Benoît Kamano dédie ses distinctions reçues à Paris au Président de la République, Chef de l’État, Mamadi Doumbouya
items.description: Le Ministre Secrétaire Général du Gouvernement, Tamba Benoît Kamano, a reçu, mardi 3 novembre 2026 à Paris, les titres d’Ambassadeur de l’Union Nations Federation et d’Ambassadeur de la Déclaration des droits de l’humanité. Il dédie cette double reconnaissance au Président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, en témoignage de sa gratitude pour la confiance placée en lui. Dans sa lettre de nomination, l’Union Nations Federation (UNF) met en avant le parcours de juriste du Ministre, ses responsabilités au service de la République de Guinée et son engagement en faveur de la coopération entre les nations, de l’accès au droit et de la dignité humaine. Ces titres lui confient une mission de représentation et de plaidoyer dans le cadre des organismes qui les décernent. Ils prolongent un engagement public dont les principaux chantiers, au Secrétariat Général du Gouvernement, portent sur la sécurisation juridique de l’action gouvernementale et la modernisation de ses méthodes de travail. Une reconnaissance portée par deux engagements internationaux L’UNF est une organisation non gouvernementale bénéficiant, depuis 2021, du statut consultatif spécial auprès du Conseil économique et social des Nations Unies (ECOSOC). Ce statut lui permet de contribuer aux travaux de cette instance dans le cadre réservé aux organisations de la société civile. La nomination est conférée par l’UNF, organisation distincte des Nations Unies. La Déclaration des droits de l’humanité est issue de travaux conduits en 2015 sous la direction de Corinne Lepage, présidente de la déclaration universelle des droits de l’humanité, Avocate et ancienne Ministre de l’Environnement français. Elle porte notamment les principes de dignité, de responsabilité et d’équité entre les générations. Signée par Sciences Po en 2022, elle nourrit une mobilisation autour de la protection des générations présentes et futures. Cette portée donne aux titres remis au Ministre une dimension d’engagement, au-delà de leur caractère honorifique. Le RISGG et le gouvernement ouvert parmi les engagements majeurs Un jalon majeur de cette action a été franchi lors du forum tenu du 14 au 16 octobre 2026 : l’institutionnalisation, sous le leadership de Tamba Benoît Kamano, du Réseau International des Secrétariats Généraux de Gouvernement (RISGG). Cette avancée donne un cadre durable à la coopération entre ces institutions et au partage de leurs expériences de coordination du travail gouvernemental. Le Ministre conduit également le processus d’adhésion de la Guinée au Partenariat pour un Gouvernement Ouvert. Cette démarche vise à renforcer la transparence de l’action publique, la participation citoyenne et la redevabilité. Elle prolonge l’ambition d’une administration plus ouverte et plus attentive aux attentes des citoyens. La confiance présidentielle au cœur de la dédicace En dédiant cette reconnaissance au Chef de l’État, le Ministre souligne la place de la confiance présidentielle dans son engagement. Il inscrit les chantiers conduits au Secrétariat Général du Gouvernement dans la vision réformatrice portée par le Président Mamadi Doumbouya, avec l’ambition de renforcer les institutions et leur capacité à servir les citoyens. Cette dédicace traduit également son adhésion à une conviction : une jeunesse consciente de ses responsabilités, compétente et intègre peut contribuer à hisser la Guinée au rang des nations respectées. La confiance qui lui est accordée appelle du travail, de la rigueur et des résultats au service du pays. Pour Tamba Benoît Kamano, l’honneur reçu engage ainsi à poursuivre les réformes et à consolider les acquis. Cette dynamique repose sur la mobilisation des équipes du Secrétariat Général du Gouvernement et des institutions partenaires, sous la coordination du Premier Ministre, Chef du gouvernement avec une même responsabilité : améliorer durablement le fonctionnement de l’État au bénéfice des Guinéens. Pour rappel Tamba Benoît Kamano est diplômé en MBA fiscalité et gestion du patrimoine à l’Institut Supérieur de Gestion (ISG), école supérieure de commerce, master 2 en droit de la propriété intellectuelle (PI), en master 1 fiscalité et droit des affaires de l’université Paris 8. Après plus de 9 ans d’expérience dans les secteurs de la banque-assurance et de la gestion de patrimoine à AXA, Allianz, Swisslife et au Crédit Agricole îles de France, il revient au pays où il travaille à l’Autorité de régulation des télécommunications (ARPT), il rejoint le Secrétariat Général du Gouvernement après un bref passage dans le secteur privé. Adjoint, puis Ministre Secrétaire Général du gouvernement, M. Kamano a conduit plusieurs réformes visant à moderniser le travail gouvernemental et à assurer l’assistance du Premier ministre, chef du gouvernement dans l’impulsion, la coordination et le contrôle de l’action gouvernementale. Élus Président du réseau international des Secrétaires Généraux de gouvernement, il porte des réformes majeures dont la déclaration d’intention non obligatoire d’utilisation de l’IA responsable et éthique pour les 13 États signataires. Nous lui souhaitions bonne chance dans ses nouveaux mandats d’ambassadeurs. C’est la Guinée qui gagne ! Service Communication et Relations Publiques du SGG.

items.title: Analysis-Midterms upended Congress but Trump still commands foreign policy
items.description: By Matt Spetalnick WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Republican Party's staggering losses at the ballot box this week have left President Donald Trump diminished in Washington and facing tougher legislative oversight and scrutiny of his agenda. But on foreign policy, he could remain unbowed. Even as Democratic lawmakers seek to rein in the Republican president when they take control of Congress, Trump will retain broad latitude to pursue his objectives on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China, during his final two years in office.

items.title: Tivaouane : TDS-SA distribue 10 000 décodeurs pour permettre aux populations de suivre les JOJ 2026
items.description: La Télédiffusion du Sénégal (TDS-SA) a entamé à Tivaouane la distribution de 10 000 décodeurs et 5 000 antennes TNT pour permettre aux populations de suivre les Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. La directrice générale de TDS-SA, Dr Aminata Sarr Ndiaye, qui conduisait la tournée ce jeudi, a indiqué que cette dotation a été acquise grâce à un investissement de 1,5 milliard de francs CFA consenti par l'État du Sénégal pour renouveler l'infrastructure de diffusion au niveau de Thiès. Cet investissement a permis le renouvellement du pylône de Thiès et l'acquisition des équipements destinés aux populations, a-t-elle précisé. « En notre qualité d'opérateur de diffusion nationale, TDS-SA a la mission d'assurer le transport et la diffusion des chaînes, mais aussi de veiller à ce que les populations aient accès à ce service », a déclaré Dr Ndiaye. La première phase de distribution a démarré à Tivaouane et se poursuivra à Popenguine, avec une priorité accordée aux foyers religieux, au nom du Chef de l'État, Son Excellence Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Le choix de ces localités s'explique, selon la DG, par le rôle important des foyers religieux et par le fait qu'elles ont été fortement impactées par la dépose du pylône de Thiès en septembre 2025. « Une expertise technique avait démontré que le pylône de 200 mètres était dans un état de vétusté avancée et présentait des risques sécuritaires. Nous l'avions remplacé par un pylône provisoire de 75 mètres, affectant la qualité du signal », a-t-elle rappelé. Les travaux de renouvellement sont en cours, a-t-elle ajouté, précisant qu'en attendant, TDS dote les populations de décodeurs et d'antennes pour accompagner la transition. Accueillie par les guides religieux qui ont salué l'effort de l'État, Dr Ndiaye a indiqué que la distribution sera appuyée par 1400 jeunes formés en 2021 par TDS-SA aux métiers du numérique et à l'installation des équipements TNT. Elle a souligné que le Sénégal a fait de la transformation numérique une priorité, sous l'impulsion du Président de la République, du Premier ministre et du ministre de la Communication, porte-parole du gouvernement, et a sollicité davantage l'accompagnement de l'État dans cette mission. Ibrahima NDIAYE Correspondant

items.title: EXCLUSIF. Kaylia Nemour : « Aujourd’hui, je suis plus forte »
items.description: Kaylia Nemour dédicacera son livre « L’Ombre de l’Or » (Anep Editions) sur le stand de l’Anep du Sila 2026, vendredi 6 novembre de 10 h à 11 h. Ecrit avec Frédéric Brindille, cet ouvrage raconte son parcours, ses épreuves et son ascension fulgurante. La championne olympique algérienne a accordé un entretien à TSA. Elle parle de son livre, de sa coach Nadia Massé , de ses objectifs, des deux médailles qu’elle a décrochées aux Mondiaux de Rotterdam 2026, de ses objectifs pour les JO 2028, de son plat algérien préféré, de ses endroits préférés à Alger… Qu’est-ce que cela vous fait d’être à nouveau en Algérie ? Kaylia Nemour : Je suis très heureuse d’être en Algérie. J’ai quand même la chance de pouvoir venir assez souvent en fonction de mon planning des entrainements. C’est toujours un plaisir de venir ici et de retrouver des gens très accueillants. Plus je viens, plus j’ai envie de revenir. Vous allez dédicacer votre livre vendredi 6 novembre au Salon international du livre d’Alger (Sila 2026). Que vont y découvrir les lecteurs de plus que ce qu’ils savent déjà sur vous ? Kaylia Nemour : Tout simplement je raconte mon histoire depuis mes débuts dans la gymnastique : comment j’ai commencé petite et tout le chemin que j’ai parcouru jusqu’aux Mondiaux 2025. Il y a des passages d’une période de ma vie très compliquée mais aussi des moments inoubliables dans ma carrière. En lisant ce livre, les gens vont rentrer dans ma tête parce que je dis vraiment ce que je pense. Les gens vont vraiment se mettre à ma place. Mon livre est facile à lire et j’espère que les lecteurs vont aimer mon histoire. Vous avez décroché deux médailles d’or il y a deux semaines aux Mondiaux de Rotterdam. C’est exceptionnel. Vous attendiez-vous à un tel succès ? Kaylia Nemour : Honnêtement, je ne m’attendais pas forcément à ce résultat final. J’avais aussi un objectif de finale et de médaille à la poutre si j’arrivais à bien faire mon mouvement, mais le premier jour je n’ai pas réussi à avoir cette médaille au concours général à cause d’une erreur. J’ai pu me remobiliser après pour les barres asymétriques et j’ai décroché l’or. J’étais très contente, en revanche avoir une médaille d’or à la poutre, c’est juste exceptionnel ! Malgré la déception en finale du concours général, vous avez su rebondir pour remporter deux médailles d’or, à la poutre et aux barres asymétriques. Comment avez-vous pu rebondir ? Kaylia Nemour : J’étais bien entourée, parce que j’avoue j’étais un peu démotivée. J’ai travaillé pendant un an pour ce concours général et il venait de m’échapper. C’était vraiment très dur mais, j’ai essayé de mettre cette déception de côté, car j’avais des finales très importantes à la poutre et aux barres asymétriques. Je me suis focalisée sur les barres puis le lendemain sur la poutre, et les résultats ont suivi. Cela a réparé mon cœur. À quoi pensez-vous au moment d’entamer une finale ? Kaylia Nemour : je suis juste concentrée sur ce que je répète tous les jours à l’entrainement. Quels sont vos objectifs pour les JO de Los Angeles 2028 Kaylia Nemour : Les Jeux olympiques c’est la plus haute compétition. Le fait que j’ai gagné deux médailles d’or, il y a deux semaines aux Mondiaux de Rotterdam, me met en confiance pour la suite du parcours. Cependant, les Jeux olympiques c’est quand même dans un an et demi. Certes, ces deux médailles reflètent le travail que j’ai accompli mais cela n’assure pas la performance des JO. Évidemment que ça met en confiance mais beaucoup de travail reste à venir. Pour les objectifs, il y a les Mondiaux en 2027 et les étapes de Coupes du monde qui vont arriver avant les JO de 2028. Viserez-vous trois médailles d’or aux JO 2028 ? Kaylia Nemour : C’est trop tôt pour s’avancer sur les objectifs mais en tout cas, je vais continuer à travailler dur pour le concours général et forcément pour les barres asymétriques et pour la poutre. Quels sont les secrets de la réussite de Kaylia Nemour ? Kaylia Nemour : Depuis toute petite, j’ai une bonne hygiène de vie : je me couche tôt, je garde une activité physique quand je n’ai pas de gymnastique et je fais attention à mon alimentation. C’est un tout qui permet de s’entrainer dur ! Après la médaille d’or aux Jeux olympiques de Paris 2024, j’ai eu une baisse de moral et de motivation mais Nadia Massé m’a montrée une autre vision de la gymnastique. Au fur et à mesure, j’ai eu de nouveaux objectifs notamment celui du concours général. Je pense qu’à présent, je suis plus forte qu’avant. Kaylia a évolué en tant que jeune femme et en tant que sportive aussi. Que vous a apporté votre nouvelle coach Nadia Massé ? Kaylia Nemour : Une autre perception de la gymnastique. Je sais pourquoi je viens, pourquoi j’effectue cet exercice. Par ailleurs, humainement parlant c’est très diffèrent. Quand on a commencé à travailler ensemble, elle m’a appris par exemple, à avoir confiance en moi. Pour moi c’est une clef, quelque chose d’important pour la performance. Vous sentez-vous aujourd’hui plus épanouie, plus heureuse ? Kaylia Nemour : C’est clair ! D’ailleurs tout le monde me le dit, que ce soit aux entrainements ou dans ma vie de tous les jours. Je reste concentrée. Le travail est exigeant mais je me suis libérée. Je reste moi-même. En gagnant la médaille d’or aux JO de Paris 2024, vous avez boosté la pratique de la gymnastique en Algérie. Quel conseil donneriez-vous aux jeunes gymnastes ? Kaylia Nemour : De rêver grand ! De pratiquer la gym avec passion, avec son cœur et en se fixant des objectifs et surtout ne pas craindre de se lancer. Pour faire du haut niveau en ce moment en Algérie, je pense que c’est le volume horaire qui manque parce qu’il y a vraiment des pépites, de belles jeunes gymnastes qui pourraient aller très loin. Une gymnaste de haut niveau doit s’entrainer entre 25 et 30 heures par semaine. Vous venez souvent en Algérie. Quels sont les endroits que vous préférez ? Kaylia Nemour : Quand je viens en Algérie, je descends principalement à Alger. J’ai été deux fois à Oran. Mes séjours s’étalent sur des périodes courtes, et très rythmées, à cause de multiples rendez-vous, sinon, j’aime beaucoup le Jardin d’Essai et la Grande-Poste. En tant qu'athlète de haut niveau, quel plat algérien vous autorisez-vous à consommer sans modération ? Kaylia Nemour : Il n’y a rien que je consomme sans modération, cependant j’aime beaucoup la rechta ! Et côté sucré, quels sont les gâteaux algériens que vous préférez ? Kaylia Nemour : Je n’aime pas tout ce qui est trop sucré. J’aime le chocolat noir, les gâteaux allégés en sucre mais pas les pâtisseries orientales qui sont trop sucrées à mon goût. items.title: British woman, unborn baby die in Nigeria; family seeks help to bring bodies home
items.description: A 40-year-old British woman who relocated to Nigeria to start a new life with her husband has died alongside her unborn baby after developing sepsis. Claire Chadwick, who was 37 weeks pregnant, reportedly suffered septic shock after her baby girl died in the womb. In a report by Daily Mail UK, Chadwick had moved to Nigeria to be with her husband, Ibrahim, and was expecting their first child together. She had built a social media following of thousands through videos documenting their relationship, religious beliefs and food challenges on TikTok and Instagram. Her death has left her family devastated, with her sister, Shannon, revealing that she is survived by her 19-year-old son in Wales, her husband and other relatives. Describing her late sister, Shannon said Claire was a funny and fiercely strong-minded woman who lived life on her own terms. “She was a woman who lived her life in her own way and she will leave a lasting impression on everyone who knew her,” she told WalesOnline. The family has since launched a GoFundMe campaign with a target of £10,000 to repatriate Claire and her unborn daughter to the United Kingdom for burial. Explaining the purpose of the fundraiser, Shannon said the family wanted to bring both bodies home so they could be laid to rest with dignity and surrounded by their loved ones. “More than anything, we want them both returned so they can be laid to rest with dignity, surrounded by the family who love them,” she said. The fundraiser has attracted widespread support, with Shannon describing the response as overwhelming. She also expressed gratitude to REST, a charity that supports families dealing with the sudden or tragic deaths of loved ones abroad. Tributes have also poured in from friends and well-wishers, who remembered Chadwick as a kind, caring and cheerful woman. One supporter recalled knowing her from childhood and described her as lovely, while another said she was devastated by the loss, remembering her as someone who always made people laugh. The family hopes to raise enough money to bring Claire and her unborn daughter back to the UK. ‘The Audacity to Dare’: TrueLife Experience challenges Ghanaians to pursue their ambitions
items.description: The 2026 TrueLife Experience has challenged Ghanaians to overcome fear, self-doubt, and other personal limitations and take deliberate steps towards achieving their ambitions. Held under the theme “The Audacity to Dare” , the two-day event is taking place at the Kempinski Hotel in Accra on November 5 and 6. The gathering brings together business executives, entrepreneurs, policymakers, professionals and emerging leaders to discuss how courage, personal development and purposeful action can help individuals translate their potential into tangible results. Convener of the initiative, Dedo Kofi, said the programme uses real-life experiences to inspire participants and provide practical lessons they can apply in their personal and professional lives. “I wanted a conference that is very relatable to people. And I believe that stories are one of the ways people can easily relate,” she said. She explained that the experiences of people who had confronted challenges and pursued their ambitions could help others navigate similar situations. According to her, having a dream does not automatically lead to success, as individuals must be prepared to work towards achieving their aspirations. “Dreams don’t happen automatically. Dreams have to be worked on. That’s why we’re talking about the audacity to dare. If people are doing that, that’s what will develop our communities and nation,” she said. She added that the willingness to pursue one’s ambitions should not be limited by age or circumstances. Keynote speaker Dzigbordi Kwaku-Dosoo urged participants to move beyond drawing inspiration from other people’s achievements and become individuals whose lives and work inspire others. Drawing on her personal journey, she highlighted the importance of developing human competence, particularly critical thinking, communication, public speaking and relationship-building skills. “You have to build the competence before you transform,” she said. Ms Kwaku-Dosoo said personal and professional growth required patience and consistent investment in self-development. She also encouraged participants to combine prayer with deliberate action, noting that progress required more than waiting for opportunities. She urged individuals to remain committed to their goals even when results were not immediate. The 2026 TrueLife Experience programme includes keynote addresses, candid conversations, practical breakout sessions known as Dare Labs and networking opportunities. The sessions are intended to provide participants with practical learning experiences, encourage collaboration and help them translate ideas into actionable plans. Other personalities associated with the gathering include business leader and African economic sovereignty advocate Sir Sam Jonah, mindset mentor Nekeya Parks and Edward Effah, founder of Fidelity Group. The event will also feature a Legacy and Honours Night to recognise individuals and organisations for their contributions to society. TrueLife Experience is a personal-development initiative that uses storytelling, conversations and shared experiences to inspire and empower individuals. The organisers say the 2026 edition seeks to move beyond motivation by providing opportunities for participants to examine challenges affecting their personal and professional growth and identify practical ways to address them.

items.title: Trump May Come to Regret His Rush Job on the Arch and Ballroom
items.description: Sign up for Inside the Trump Presidency , a newsletter featuring coverage of the second Trump term. When Donald Trump gathered news crews and administration officials at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool earlier this week, it was obvious that he wanted to offer a strong closing pitch ahead of Election Day. But that message, which involved a long digression about the pool’s pipes, fit a pattern that has come to define his second term. While everyone else talks about the Iran war and the cost of groceries, Trump remains focused on what he knows best: real estate. That didn’t change following Tuesday’s Republican wipeout. Yesterday, he gave reporters a tour of the White House ballroom site, talking up a “special vein” in the marble and waving off questions about the election. The president’s aspirations for remaking the nation’s capital have never been popular among voters. To realize his architectural ambitions, he has skipped legislative approval, moved around federal funds, and had Justice Department lawyers test the patience of federal judges. The embarrassment of the midterms is unlikely to slow him down—on the contrary, Trump seems focused above all on speeding up his construction projects. He is more than halfway through building the ballroom, plans to start construction soon on the United States Triumphal Arch, intends to break ground this month on a championship-grade golf course on public land, and continues to effectively hold the Kennedy Center hostage. (And that’s just a partial list. The administration has yet to unveil design plans for a National Garden of American Heroes in D.C., for example, but they’re probably coming.) Democrats have loudly complained about these projects, but until now, they haven’t had much power, outside of the courts, to stop them. The next Congress, however, is poised to use its strongest weapon against the president’s building spree: a few lines tucked into a spending bill. Legal experts told me that although Democrats will likely try to use legislation, oversight hearings, and appropriations to rein in Trump’s Washington, D.C., makeover, they are most likely to succeed by focusing on spending. (This approach carries its own drawbacks. It could lead to a standoff that culminates with a government shutdown.) How the fight plays out could test just how much Trump believes that his projects will define and outlast his presidency, as well as what he might be willing to risk in that process. The White House did not respond to my requests for comment. “He clearly thinks that this is how he wants to be remembered, as building these projects,” David Super, a Georgetown University law professor, told me. But defending them could be costly. Trump has already threatened to become “Mr. Veto” in January, so it’s probable that he’ll block any legislation that tries to restrict or terminate his projects. Yet Paul Schiff Berman, a law professor at George Washington University, told me that the Kennedy Center generally receives bipartisan support and could be the rare case in which enough lawmakers would back “common-sense” statutory amendments that strengthen protections for the institution. When Democrats control congressional committees and have the ability to subpoena witnesses, they may choose to overwhelm Trump with oversight hearings that could probe who is paying for Trump’s ballroom, the amount of money federal agencies have spent on the arch, and how the projects were approved in the first place. But as he is likely to do with investigations into corruption and other Democratic targets, Trump could stop administration officials from testifying, forcing that matter to go to court. Ultimately, there’s only so much that hearings can accomplish: They can help expose collusion or mismanagement, but an oversight hearing can’t send a construction crew home or halt funding for a building project. [ Read: The rush-job presidency ] The appropriations process is where Democrats have a real opening. They could add language to spending bills that restricts how federal money is used for these projects. Trump had previously told a group of donors that his planned 250-foot arch was fully paid for, suggesting that remaining private funds donated to his White House ballroom project could be diverted to the arch’s construction. But officials plan to use $15 million from the National Endowment for the Humanities for the structure, which is estimated to cost $100 million. The ballroom has also required hundreds of millions of federal dollars to support its ballooning costs. Even if private donors were paying for every stone of the triumphal arch, the government still must review plans, supervise construction, and ultimately operate the site. “All of those are expenditures of federal funds,” Super said, “and if Congress says those are all impermissible, then the archway can’t move.” Then again, writing a restriction would invite another question: What happens if the Trump administration ignores it? That could mean yet another court fight. Democratic House appropriators are already discussing ways to halt or restrict Trump’s projects, Representative Chellie Pingree, the top Democrat on the Subcommittee on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies, told me. Pingree said that those efforts would be among the priorities for Democrats when they assume the House majority in January, along with efforts to restore the Kennedy Center’s integrity and independence. At the arts institution, where $257 million has already been appropriated for renovations, lawmakers have the option to claw back whatever portion hasn’t been legally committed to contractors, Super, the Georgetown professor, told me. The catch: Trump could veto a spending bill, too, over that or any other issue. In normal times, a government-funding fight probably wouldn’t focus on a monument or arts center. Now there’s a decent chance that the building projects will figure into negotiations with the White House. “That depends on the willingness of Trump on the one hand and Democratic leadership on the other hand to shut down the government over one of these pet projects,” Berman said. The first chance for a fight could come in December, in the lame-duck period, when the current funding measure is set to expire. The outgoing Congress could negotiate some of these issues then, but Super thinks that lawmakers could extend funding into February or March, leaving the bigger disputes for the new Congress. And Democrats may conclude that to make progress on important issues, letting Trump build a golf course or sculpture garden is a worthwhile trade. “Nobody really likes shutting down the government,” Berman said. Trump has every incentive to speedrun his projects before the new Congress begins. And he is. This afternoon, the triumphal arch is expected to get its final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, one of several federal bodies that Trump has packed with allies as he has pursued aesthetic changes in D.C. The administration has indicated that the Department of the Interior could sign off on the project today, too, and that construction preparations could begin immediately after that. Two lawsuits over the work are playing out, so a federal judge could potentially stop it before it begins. In one of these cases, the judge recently pressed the administration about why it felt so rushed to start construction. But the answer is obvious. At the Kennedy Center, Trump and his allies are still seeking a two-year shutdown as the institution fights a lawsuit brought by Representative Joyce Beatty, an ex-officio member of its board who is challenging the president’s overhaul. A federal judge has set a hearing for later this month to consider lifting the preliminary injunction that has temporarily blocked the institution from closing for renovation. But because Trump has threatened to not proceed with construction unless he’s allowed to put his name on the building, this fight has taken on an existential quality: Beatty and others are worried that Trump may leave the Kennedy Center an empty shell, and he has said that it might need to be “ripped down” without his help. The golf course’s closure is imminent. The Trump administration announced that East Potomac Golf Links will shut down on November 15 for redevelopment, a move that would close a federally run park near the National Mall to locals who jog, fish, cycle, and picnic there. Normally, a plan like Trump’s would take years, for better and for worse. But the administration already intends to present its plans to the National Capital Planning Commission next month, even as it fights a lawsuit filed by golfers and preservationists in federal court. Some observers are wary of what else might happen from now to January. Notably, the administration is trying to water down historic-preservation rules that would apply to—and likely slow down—most of these building projects. Charles Birnbaum, the president and CEO of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, which is suing the government over Trump’s renovations to the Reflecting Pool, told me he believes that the next few weeks could bring a “tsunami” of activity from the White House to speed through as much construction as possible before January. He brought up the example of the D.C. golf course, where the administration has strained to convince a judge that recent tree removals were part of already-planned maintenance and not related to Trump’s redesign. “In the way that the administration went in and felled trees on the Columbus Day weekend, I think based on past performance, we should expect this to be a rough ride between now and the end of the year,” he said. Whether they’re complete or not, Trump’s projects will likely be an issue for the next president. A Democratic administration could take down the arch (although Trump could sue as a private citizen), remove Trump’s name from buildings (ditto), and turn the ballroom into offices (ditto again)—all while invoking the same expansive view of presidential power that Trump has relied on to remake the city without securing congressional authorization. “If we teach the Democrats that lesson,” Super told me, “they will do exactly the same thing in reverse.” If the rules didn’t apply to the builder, should they apply to the demolition crew?

items.title: ADC crisis: No one is above party constitution, Nafiu Bala tells Mark-led exco
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike Hon. Nafiu Bala Gombe, National Chairman of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), has declared that no political party leader is above the party’s constitution, following the Federal High Court judgment on the party’s leadership dispute. Gombe said the judgment reinforced the principle that leadership positions in political parties must emerge through lawful and constitutionally recognised procedures, not imposition or political expediency, insisting that courts must intervene when parties disregard their own rules. In a statement reacting to the judgment in Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025, involving him, the ADC and four others, Gombe commended the trial judge for what he described as an independent, impartial and courageous handling of the politically sensitive dispute. “With profound respect for the Bench, and with a deep sense of duty to the administration of justice in Nigeria, I most respectfully commend the Federal High Court and the trial Judge for the independent, impartial, and intellectually rigorous manner in which His Lordship handled and determined the above-referenced matter,” he said. Describing the case as a major test of judicial independence, Gombe said it raised critical questions about party autonomy, internal democracy, constitutional supremacy and the regulatory responsibilities of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). “By subjecting the question of leadership emergence to constitutional and statutory scrutiny, rather than to political expediency, His Lordship affirmed a foundational principle of Nigerian jurisprudence: political parties are not above their own constitutions, and the Electoral Act is not a mere suggestion,” he stated. On the obligation of political parties to obey their internal rules, Gombe said courts had a duty to intervene where established procedures were disregarded. “Where a party’s constitution prescribes a procedure for succession and leadership, that procedure must be obeyed. Where a political party fails to comply with the rules, procedures, and constitutional provisions laid down for its own governance, the court is duty-bound to intervene in order to safeguard democracy, uphold the rule of law, and prevent anarchy. “No man is above the law, and no man is below it,” he declared. The ADC chairman said the judgment went beyond the immediate contest between the parties, arguing that it demonstrated that the judiciary could withstand political pressure and decide cases strictly on their merits. “It restores public confidence that a judge can still decide on the law and the facts alone, uninfluenced by political pressure, media commentary, or the weight of personalities involved in the suit. “It affirms that leadership must emerge through lawful process, not through imposition, and that aggrieved members have a legitimate right to seek redress in court rather than resort to self-help. It reassures ordinary Nigerians that the court remains the last hope of the common man, and indeed, of every man,” he added. Citing the judicial principle that justice must not only be done but must manifestly be seen to be done, Gombe said the judge’s conduct in the case reflected that standard. He also commended the judge for demonstrating patience, erudition and firmness in handling the dispute, while praising his legal team for its diligence and commitment throughout the proceedings. Gombe further thanked supporters across the country for their solidarity, loyalty and prayers, urging the judiciary to sustain its commitment to impartial justice, constitutional democracy and the rule of law. He insisted that political parties must respect their constitutions and ensure that leadership emerges through lawful procedures rather than imposition. items.title: Queen Máxima engages patients on how PharmAccess’ NkwaPlus is changing chronic disease care
items.description: Queen Máxima of the Netherlands has engaged three patients living with chronic diseases at Manna Mission Hospital in Accra to understand how PharmAccess Ghana’s NkwaPlus digital healthcare platform is improving access to medical care and helping them manage their health alongside their financial responsibilities. The Queen, who visited the hospital in her capacity as the United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Advocate for Financial Health, was particularly interested in why patients were willing to pay for digital healthcare services despite being covered by the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS). The engagement brought together three patients, Margaret, Dorinda and Famos, who are receiving treatment at the hospital under a Value-Based Care initiative jointly designed by PharmAccess, the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and the Christian Health Association of Ghana (CHAG). Country Director of PharmAccess Foundation, Dr. Maxwell Antwi, who moderated the engagement, explained that the initiative allows patients to receive medical attention beyond the hospital through NkwaPlus. “They are three patients who are receiving care in this hospital. They are also all covered by the National Health Insurance Scheme, which is our social health insurance scheme,” he explained. “But they are also being seen on the app, so that from their market, home and offices, they can take their blood pressure and send it to the doctors, and then the medical team can take care of them. And when need be, they come in for care.” Queen questions patients on paying for NkwaPlus Leading the conversation, Queen Máxima sought to understand the patients’ motivation for enrolling on NkwaPlus when the digital monitoring service was not yet covered by the NHIS. The dialogue was designed to explore the experiences of patients receiving care through NkwaPlus, particularly how remote monitoring affects their ability to work, earn an income and meet their household responsibilities. It also examined the financial burden of chronic disease management, including the out-of-pocket costs of digital healthcare services and the choices families face when medical expenses compete with other essential needs. How NkwaPlus supports chronic disease management The NkwaPlus platform forms part of the Value-Based Care initiative, which combines periodic hospital consultations with digital monitoring between visits. Through the platform, patients living with conditions such as hypertension and diabetes can check their blood pressure at home or work and share the readings with medical professionals for review. This enables healthcare teams to monitor patients between hospital appointments and determine when they need further medical attention. While the NHIS covers periodic hospital consultations under the initiative, patients currently pay out of pocket for the digital monitoring service. The arrangement has brought attention to the need for a financing model that makes digital healthcare more accessible to people living with chronic diseases. Value-Based Care pilot records improved patient outcomes The implementation of the Value-Based Care initiative, which incorporates NkwaPlus, has recorded improvements in hypertension management, with the proportion of participating patients whose blood pressure was under control increasing from 50 per cent to 57.1 per cent after 12 months. More than 90 per cent of patients participating in the pilot also indicated that they would recommend the service. The initiative seeks to improve patient outcomes while addressing the growing cost of managing chronic diseases, particularly hypertension and diabetes. PharmAccess, the NHIA and CHAG are working towards a financing approach that would place greater emphasis on improved patient outcomes rather than the number of healthcare services provided. Although outcome-based payments have not yet begun, the pilot has introduced non-financial incentives for healthcare providers, including early reimbursement of claims and early re-credentialing. One of the proposed next steps is for the NHIA to develop a reimbursement tariff for digital healthcare services such as NkwaPlus, which patients currently finance themselves. The Queen’s interaction with the patients formed part of her broader visit to Ghana, which focuses on improving financial health and protecting households against unexpected expenses, including the cost of medical care.

items.title: Queen Máxima pushes for NHIS coverage of digital healthcare like NkwaPlus to reduce patients’ medical costs
items.description: Queen Máxima of the Netherlands has called for greater efforts to reduce out-of-pocket healthcare expenses in Ghana, particularly for patients living with chronic diseases who continue to pay for some medical services despite having health insurance. The Queen believes Ghana’s National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) must evolve to accommodate digital healthcare services that allow patients to receive medical attention from home without making frequent visits to hospitals. Speaking during a policy dialogue with healthcare providers and policymakers at Manna Mission Hospital in Accra, Queen Máxima expressed interest in how Ghana could improve its health insurance system to reduce the financial burden on patients. The engagement followed her interaction with three patients receiving treatment under a Value-Based Care initiative jointly developed by PharmAccess Ghana, the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and the Christian Health Association of Ghana (CHAG). The initiative combines hospital consultations covered by the NHIS with digital monitoring through PharmAccess’ NkwaPlus platform. Queen Máxima, who is visiting Ghana as the United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Advocate for Financial Health, said health insurance remains critical to protecting households against unexpected medical expenses. “Having health insurance is a very important part because it’s one of the very big items of unforeseen costs for people,” she said. She acknowledged Ghana’s progress in expanding health insurance coverage but expressed concern that patients still incurred substantial expenses when accessing healthcare. “In not many countries in Africa do you have quite good insurance coverage on the health side. And if you do, I know that still a lot of people pay out of pocket for a lot of things, so it is still a big-ticket item for patients,” she observed. The Queen said she was interested in understanding how Ghana could build on its health insurance system to make healthcare more affordable and efficient. “I want to learn from the Ghanaian example how you’ve seen this evolving and, looking into all the out-of-pocket side, how we can actually make that less, because that’s always hurting the financial health of people,” she said. Queen explores expansion of NHIS to digital healthcare Country Director of PharmAccess Ghana, Dr. Maxwell Antwi, who facilitated the engagement, explained that the discussion with patients had highlighted the relationship between health insurance, household finances and digital healthcare. “We’ve just had a very interesting discussion with the patients, really speaking about what insurance means to them at the individual and household level,” he said. He also highlighted the need to expand healthcare financing to accommodate digital services that enable patients to receive medical attention without frequently travelling to hospitals. “There is also the need to move this on to include digital care, so that they don’t always have to come to the hospital but can be taken care of from home,” he explained. The NkwaPlus platform allows patients living with hypertension and diabetes to monitor their conditions remotely and share their readings with healthcare professionals. The technology forms part of the Value-Based Care initiative being piloted by PharmAccess, the NHIA and CHAG to improve the management of chronic diseases while reducing avoidable healthcare expenditure. The initiative has recorded improvements in hypertension management, with the proportion of participating patients whose blood pressure was under control increasing from 50 per cent at baseline to 57.1 per cent after 12 months. More than 90 per cent of participating patients also indicated that they would recommend the service. However, while hospital consultations under the initiative are covered by the NHIS, remote monitoring through NkwaPlus is not yet included in the Scheme’s reimbursement arrangements. NHIA defends increased investment in healthcare Responding during the dialogue, the Chief Executive Officer of the NHIA, Dr. Victor Asare Bampoe said Ghana had made significant progress in increasing domestic financing for healthcare following the removal of the cap on the National Health Insurance Levy. He explained that the decision had made additional resources available to the Scheme, allowing it to expand coverage, improve reimbursements and increase tariffs paid to healthcare providers. The NHIA CEO said the government was also pursuing a shift in how healthcare investments are viewed. “The first is the mindset shift, so that they see health not as a cost centre but as an investment centre,” he explained. He maintained that the additional financial resources had strengthened the Scheme’s ability to deliver healthcare services, but acknowledged that greater attention must now be given to the outcomes achieved with those investments. “That’s all on the input side. That’s all on the volume side. Where our friends then come in is, what are we actually paying for with that money?” he questioned. He said this was why the Value-Based Care initiative had become relevant to the Authority’s long-term healthcare financing strategy. “That’s why value-based care is something that is interesting for us, because there will come a time when we will not be able to get all those funds,” he said. “But then if we have results, that will speak for itself. So that’s where Ghana is now. We are at those crossroads.” PharmAccess and partners seek reforms in healthcare payments The policy dialogue brought together the NHIA leadership, PharmAccess Ghana Country Director Dr. Maxwell Antwi, PharmAccess Chief Executive Officer Dr Nicole Spieker, CHAG Executive Director Dr. Peter Yeboah and Manna Mission Hospital head Linda Ablorh. A major issue under consideration was how Ghana could move towards paying healthcare providers based on improvements in patient outcomes rather than solely on the number of services delivered. Under the Value-Based Care pilot, the NHIA and its partners have introduced non-financial incentives, including early reimbursement of claims and early re-credentialing, to encourage healthcare providers to prioritise patient outcomes. The discussions also identified two proposed next steps: developing reimbursement tariffs for improved patient outcomes in managing chronic diseases and introducing NHIS payment arrangements for digital healthcare services such as NkwaPlus. The proposals are intended to make digital healthcare more accessible while encouraging providers to deliver measurable improvements in patient health. Speaking separately to JoyNews, CHAG Executive Director Dr. Peter Yeboah said the approach could help Ghana make better use of its healthcare investments. “The key paradigm shift today is a shift from the volume of healthcare services to the value that we derive from that,” he said. “We should not be too fixated about the number or the volume of services that people utilise, but we should ask ourselves who is benefiting and what real benefit is coming out of that.” He maintained that improved patient outcomes and financial protection must remain central to healthcare reforms. “The case is simple. Health is not a cost; it is an investment,” he stressed. Queen Máxima’s engagement with the healthcare policymakers formed part of her four-day visit to Ghana, which focused on improving financial security and protecting households against unexpected expenses, including the cost of medical care.
